name: Jinrai

answers.ninjo: Jinrai tells himself he has left the ashigaru life behind, but he still drills footwork every morning before the farmers wake, and last month he spent two days teaching a village headman's son how to hold a spear.
answers.standout_quality: He preaches forgiveness to farmers and merchants while his jaw tightens whenever a samurai enters the room, and he knows they can see it.
answers.accomplishment: Jinrai converted a bandit who had burned two granaries, and now that man tends crops in a village near Beiden while Jinrai takes a longer road to avoid the merchant who owned them.
answers.challenge: When he decides a farmer needs to learn spearwork or a village headman's judgment is wrong, Jinrai teaches or corrects them regardless of what he promised to do that day.
answers.peace: In the village temple's side room, Jinrai kneels before a low table arranging cut stems—a priest's discards, market flowers past their prime—rotating each one until the angles speak to each other, his shoulders dropping lower with each placement until his breathing settles into the rhythm of the work itself.
answers.fear: When Jinrai performs the evening sutras in an empty temple, he cannot shake the certainty that his dead grandmother—who bore a samurai's bastard son in shame—watches him teach forgiveness to the very class that destroyed her, waiting to see if he will finally break.
answers.past: He trained ashigaru recruits in the rice paddies outside Beiden, and three of them died in his first real command because he gave the order to hold a bridge too long.
answers.known_for: In a village near Beiden, Jinrai converted a bandit who had burned two granaries, and now the bandit works the fields while Jinrai avoids the merchant whose grain stores those were.
answers.prized_possession: Jinrai's sandals are worn through at the heel on the right foot, and he refuses to replace them though he passes through towns that sell better ones.
answers.group_history: When the group stops to make camp, Jinrai always volunteers to gather firewood and walks farther than necessary to avoid watching them eat their evening meal together.
answers.raised_by: Kakita Tanomo raised him in the ashigaru barracks outside Beiden, and Jinrai has spent fifteen years trying to teach forgiveness while still drilling the footwork Tanomo beat into his spine.
answers.stress_reaction: When the weight of responsibility presses down, Jinrai stops speaking mid-sentence and begins drilling footwork—the ashigaru drills from Beiden, precise and punishing—until his legs burn and his mind goes quiet, which troubles him because it means the monk is losing ground to the soldier.
answers.relationships:
Agasha Yagorô (Dragon) — Agasha Yagorô brings him maps of the Dragon territories and asks which villages need teachers, and Jinrai accepts them though he knows Yagorô is testing whether he will finally agree that some people deserve enlightenment more than others.
Tasuoki (Ganzu Guardian Tradition) — Tasuoki stopped him on the road to ask if the Perfect Land teaching truly applied to warriors, and Jinrai spent an hour explaining that it did, but he has not walked that direction again.

bio:
Jinrai is a former ashigaru turned monk, now a wandering teacher of the Perfect Land Sect. He believes that all people are equal in the eyes of enlightenment, rejecting the Celestial Order and spreading the sect's teachings to the common folk. Though he preaches peace, he struggles to let go of his resentment toward the samurai, finding it difficult to forgive their oppression.

His presence radiates determination and purpose, and he speaks passionately and inspiringly, ensuring that his words move those who listen. However, he suppresses hope, fearing that his efforts will ultimately change nothing. Though he enjoys luxuries when offered, he tries to live simply, though he sometimes indulges in a warm bed or fine meal.

Jinrai once converted a violent bandit to the Perfect Land Sect, proving the power of faith over force. He finds peace in chanting sutras, yet he secretly longs to be free of responsibility, growing weary of carrying the burden of leadership. His view of mortality is simple — his life is a sacrifice worth making if it furthers the cause of enlightenment.
